anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description: Definition: Root cause located at the user-submitted workload semantics, where application-issued statements, stored routines, or transaction boundaries are written in a way that forces the engine to process more data, more rows, or longer transactions than the business requirement actually needs. This is the highest layer of root-cause attribution and is independent of the optimizer, configuration, and hardware. Observable phenomena: long-tail statement latency reported by engine-level statement-statistics views, the same statements appearing repeatedly in slow-query logs, individual transactions holding resources for unusually long periods, application-level timeouts and retries, and session traces showing wide row scans, repeated round-trips, or oversized result sets. Possible contributing factors: predicates that are not index-friendly or that wrap indexed columns inside functions, projection of unnecessary columns, unintended Cartesian joins, sub-optimal join order written by the application, repeated single-row access patterns produced by object-relational frameworks, missing or overly broad filter conditions, oversized in-list predicates, excessive batch sizes, transactions kept open across user think-time or external service calls, and ad-hoc analytical queries running directly against transactional tables.

entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with a general engine-level execution problem surfaced by the official error catalogue, but its precise trigger must be interpreted together with workload context and surrounding evidence.
entry.solution_guidance: Review the surrounding workload, official description, and engine state to determine whether the issue is rooted in SQL logic, resource pressure, configuration, or environmental instability.
